name: Zhou conquest of the Shang
summary: The Zhou, a western vassal people of the Wei valley, overthrew the Shang dynasty that had ruled the North China Plain for some five centuries. King Wu of Zhou destroyed the army of the last Shang king, Di Xin, at Muye in c. 1046 BC, and his brother the Duke of Zhou crushed a great Shang revolt a few years later. The victors justified their rule as the Mandate of Heaven, an idea that framed Chinese politics for three thousand years.

steps.label: c. 1059 to 1050 BC
steps.title: Zhou rises in the west
steps.text: Under nominal Shang overlordship, King Wen of Zhou built up a power base in the Wei valley, conquered the neighbouring state of Chong and moved his capital east to Feng. He then struck across the mountains at Li in Shanxi, within reach of the Shang heartland, and gathered allied peoples of the west. The map's border data shows the whole Chinese core as one polity, coloured here for the Shang overlord.

fronts.label: Zhou and Shang spheres, c. 1050 BC

events.name: Zhou conquest of Chong
events.text: King Wen took Chong, a Shang ally guarding the Wei valley, and built his new capital Feng nearby.

steps.label: c. 1048 BC
steps.title: Gathering at Mengjin
steps.text: King Wu succeeded his father and led the Zhou army east down the Yellow River to the ford at Mengjin. Tradition says some eight hundred lords gathered there to join him, but Wu judged the moment premature and withdrew. Inside the Shang court, Di Xin was alienating his own nobles and spending his armies on wars against the Eastern Yi.

events.name: Assembly at Mengjin
events.text: The allied lords rallied to Zhou at the river crossing, but King Wu turned back to wait.

steps.label: c. 1046 BC
steps.title: Battle of Muye
steps.text: Two years later King Wu crossed at Mengjin with his chariots, the commander Jiang Ziya and contingents from western peoples, and marched on the Shang capital at Chaoge. On the plain of Muye the Shang army, much of it pressed captives, broke and turned on its own side. Di Xin set fire to his palace and died, and King Wu proclaimed that Heaven had transferred its mandate to Zhou.

moves.label: Zhou army crosses and marches on Chaoge
Shang army goes out to Muye

events.name: Battle of Muye
events.text: The Zhou coalition routed the Shang army in a single day; the traditional date of 1046 BC comes from modern chronology work and is still debated.

events.name: Fall of Chaoge
events.text: Di Xin burned himself in his palace, ending the Shang dynasty.

steps.label: c. 1042 to 1039 BC
steps.title: Revolt of the Three Guards
steps.text: After King Wu died, the Shang prince Wu Geng, left to rule the old capital, rose in revolt with two of Wu's own brothers and the eastern states of Yan and Pugu. The Duke of Zhou, regent for the young King Cheng, led an eastern expedition that took about three years to crush them. Zhou then built a second capital at Chengzhou near Luoyang and settled royal kinsmen across the east as fief holders.

moves.label: Shang rebels and the Three Guards

events.name: Suppression of Wu Geng
events.text: The Duke of Zhou killed Wu Geng and Prince Guan and exiled Prince Cai, ending Shang resistance.

events.name: Founding of Chengzhou
events.text: A new eastern capital at Luoyang let Zhou watch over the conquered plain.

name: Trojan War (legend)
summary: The Trojan War is a legend, told centuries later in Homer's Iliad and Odyssey: a Greek (Achaean) coalition under Agamemnon besieged Troy for ten years to recover Helen and finally took it by the trick of the wooden horse. Whether a real war lies behind it is unknown, but archaeology at Hisarlik in northwest Turkey shows a rich Bronze Age city that was destroyed more than once around 1250 to 1180 BC, and Hittite letters mention Wilusa (Ilios) and the Ahhiyawa (Achaeans). The dates used here are traditional, after the ancient scholar Eratosthenes.

steps.label: c. 1194 BC (legend)
steps.title: The fleet sails from Aulis
steps.text: In the legend, the Trojan prince Paris carried off Helen, wife of Menelaus of Sparta, and Agamemnon of Mycenae raised a fleet of more than a thousand ships at Aulis. The Achaeans crossed the Aegean, landed on the beach below Troy and fortified a camp by their ships. This is myth, not recorded history, though the late Bronze Age Mycenaean kingdoms and Troy were both real.

events.name: Landing at Troy
events.text: In Homer's story the Achaeans fought their way ashore and beached their ships at the mouth of the Scamander.

steps.label: c. 1194 to 1185 BC (legend)
steps.title: Siege and the Iliad
steps.text: The Iliad covers a few weeks in the tenth year of a long stalemate on the plain between the city and the Achaean camp. Hector drove the Achaeans back to their ships while Achilles sulked, until Achilles returned to battle and killed Hector. These scenes are poetry composed around 750 BC; no source confirms them.

events.name: Death of Hector
events.text: In the Iliad Achilles killed Hector before the walls of Troy, the climax of Homer's poem.

steps.label: c. 1184 BC (legend); c. 1180 BC (archaeology)
steps.title: Fall of Troy
steps.text: In the later legend, the Achaeans pretended to sail away to Tenedos and left a wooden horse with soldiers hidden inside, which the Trojans dragged into their city. That night Troy was opened and burned. At Hisarlik, the layer archaeologists call Troy VIIa was destroyed by fire around 1180 BC, during the wider Late Bronze Age collapse, but who destroyed it is unknown.

moves.label: Feigned withdrawal to Tenedos and return

events.name: Sack of Troy
events.text: Legend says Troy fell to the wooden horse; archaeology shows a burned city at Hisarlik around 1180 BC.

name: Assyrian and Kushite wars for Egypt and the Levant
summary: From 744 BC the reformed Neo-Assyrian army of Tiglath-Pileser III and his successors conquered the Aramean and Israelite kingdoms of the Levant, while the Kushite kings of Napata in Nubia made themselves pharaohs of Egypt. For eighty years the two empires fought through the small states between them, until Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal invaded Egypt itself and sacked Thebes in 663 BC. Kush withdrew to Nubia for good, but Assyria had overstretched, and within fifty years both Egypt and Babylon had broken free and Nineveh had fallen.

steps.label: 744 to 732 BC
steps.title: Tiglath-Pileser III marches west
steps.text: Tiglath-Pileser III seized the Assyrian throne in 745 BC and built a standing army that subdued the Neo-Hittite and Aramean states of Syria. When Damascus and Israel formed a coalition against him, he marched down the coast to the border of Egypt in 734 BC and then took Damascus in 732 BC, deporting its people. In the far south, the Kushite king Kashta already ruled Upper Egypt from Napata.

events.name: Fall of Damascus
events.text: Assyria captured Damascus, executed King Rezin and ended the Aramean kingdom.

steps.label: c. 728 BC
steps.title: Piye conquers Egypt
steps.text: Egypt was split among rival Libyan princes, and Tefnakht of Sais was pushing south up the Nile. The Kushite king Piye sailed and marched north from Napata, took Hermopolis and stormed Memphis, and the Delta rulers submitted to him. Under his brother Shabaka the Kushite 25th Dynasty ruled all of Egypt, putting a new power on Assyria's southwest flank.

events.name: Siege of Memphis
events.text: Piye stormed Memphis from the river side, and the princes of the Delta submitted to him.

steps.label: 722 to 720 BC
steps.title: Samaria and Raphia
steps.text: Shalmaneser V and then Sargon II took Samaria after a long siege and deported the people of the northern Kingdom of Israel. When Gaza rebelled with Egyptian help, Sargon defeated the rebels and an Egyptian force at Raphia, the first clash between Assyria and the Nile kingdom.

moves.label: Sargon's army to the Egyptian border

events.name: Fall of Samaria
events.text: Assyria ended the northern Kingdom of Israel and deported much of its population.

events.name: Battle of Raphia
events.text: Sargon II beat Gaza and its Egyptian allies on the frontier of Egypt.

steps.label: 701 BC
steps.title: Sennacherib and Hezekiah
steps.text: Hezekiah of Judah, Sidon and the Philistine cities rebelled, counting on Kushite Egypt. Sennacherib swept down the coast, defeated the Egyptian and Kushite relief army at Eltekeh and stormed Lachish, then shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem. Jerusalem was not taken, but Hezekiah paid heavy tribute and the Levant stayed Assyrian.

events.name: Battle of Eltekeh
events.text: Sennacherib defeated the army sent from Egypt to relieve the rebels.

events.name: Siege of Lachish
events.text: Assyria stormed Judah's second city, a victory carved on the walls of Sennacherib's palace at Nineveh.

events.name: Blockade of Jerusalem
events.text: The city held out, and Hezekiah bought peace with tribute while remaining an Assyrian vassal.

steps.label: 674 to 671 BC
steps.title: Esarhaddon invades Egypt
steps.text: Taharqa, the most powerful Kushite pharaoh, kept stirring revolt in the Levant. A first Assyrian invasion was thrown back at the Egyptian border in 674 BC, but in 671 BC Esarhaddon crossed Sinai with camels supplied by Arab allies and fought his way to Memphis. Memphis fell, Taharqa's family was captured, and Taharqa fled south.

events.name: Assyrian repulse at the border
events.text: Babylonian records note an Assyrian defeat in Egypt, a rare setback for Esarhaddon.

events.name: Fall of Memphis
events.text: Esarhaddon took Memphis and installed Assyrian governors and vassal princes in Lower Egypt.

steps.label: 669 to 666 BC
steps.title: Ashurbanipal and Taharqa
steps.text: Taharqa returned and retook Memphis, and Esarhaddon died at Harran on his way to deal with him. His son Ashurbanipal sent an army that beat Taharqa in the Delta and pushed up the Nile to Thebes. Assyria ruled Egypt through Delta princes such as Necho I of Sais, whose loyalty was shaky.

events.name: Battle of Karbaniti
events.text: Ashurbanipal's army defeated Taharqa in the Delta and retook Memphis; the exact site is unknown.

steps.label: 664 to 663 BC
steps.title: Sack of Thebes
steps.text: Taharqa's successor Tantamani marched north, retook Memphis and killed Necho I. Ashurbanipal answered with a full invasion: Tantamani fled, and the Assyrians sacked Thebes, the ancient religious capital of Egypt, carrying off its treasures. Kush never again ruled Egypt, and Necho's son Psamtik I, at first an Assyrian vassal, soon made Egypt independent.

events.name: Sack of Thebes
events.text: Assyria plundered Thebes, ending Kushite rule in Egypt.

events.name: Psamtik I in power
events.text: Assyria's Saite vassal became pharaoh and reunified Egypt, breaking away from Assyria within a decade.

name: Persian conquests of Cyrus and Cambyses
summary: Cyrus II, king of the small Persian realm of Anshan, overthrew his Median overlord Astyages in 550 BC and then defeated, one after another, the allied powers that might have stopped him: Lydia in 547 BC and Babylon in 539 BC. His son Cambyses II completed the work by conquering Egypt in 525 BC. In 25 years the Persians built the Achaemenid Empire, the largest state the world had yet seen, stretching from the Aegean to Central Asia and the Nile.

steps.label: 553 to 550 BC
steps.title: Cyrus overthrows Media
steps.text: Cyrus, a Persian vassal king of the Medes, rebelled against his grandfather Astyages. When Astyages marched into Persis, part of his army mutinied under the noble Harpagus and handed him over, and Cyrus then took the Median capital Ecbatana with its treasury. The Median lands from the Zagros to the Halys river in Anatolia passed to the Persians.

events.name: Battle of Pasargadae
events.text: Astyages' army defected to Cyrus, and the Median king was captured.

events.name: Capture of Ecbatana
events.text: Cyrus took the Median capital and its treasure, inheriting Media's empire.

steps.label: 547 to 546 BC
steps.title: Croesus and the fall of Sardis
steps.text: Croesus of Lydia, allied with Babylon, Egypt and Sparta, crossed the Halys to strike first. After an indecisive battle at Pteria he went home for the winter, but Cyrus followed him straight to Sardis, routed the Lydian cavalry with his camels and took the citadel. Harpagus then subdued the Greek cities of Ionia.

events.name: Battle of Pteria
events.text: Neither king won outright, and Croesus withdrew to Sardis expecting no winter campaign.

events.name: Siege of Sardis
events.text: Cyrus took the Lydian capital and captured Croesus, making Anatolia Persian.

steps.label: 539 BC
steps.title: Fall of Babylon
steps.text: After campaigns in the east, Cyrus turned on the Neo-Babylonian Empire, whose king Nabonidus had alienated the priests of Marduk. Cyrus beat the Babylonian army at Opis on the Tigris, Sippar opened its gates, and his general Gobryas entered Babylon without a fight. Syria and Palestine came with it, and Cyrus allowed exiled peoples, including the Jews, to return home.

events.name: Battle of Opis
events.text: Cyrus destroyed the main Babylonian army near the Tigris.

events.name: Fall of Babylon
events.text: Babylon surrendered almost without fighting, and Cyrus entered as a restorer of order.

steps.label: 530 BC
steps.title: Death of Cyrus
steps.text: Cyrus spent his last years on the steppe frontier of Central Asia. In 530 BC he was killed fighting the Massagetae nomads east of the Caspian, according to Herodotus by the army of their queen Tomyris. His son Cambyses II succeeded him and prepared to attack Egypt, the last great independent power of the Near East.

events.name: Death of Cyrus
events.text: Cyrus fell in battle with the Massagetae; the site is unknown.

steps.label: 525 BC
steps.title: Cambyses conquers Egypt
steps.text: Cambyses gathered a Phoenician and Cypriot fleet, and Arab chiefs supplied water for his army's crossing of Sinai. At Pelusium on the eastern edge of the Delta he crushed the army of the new pharaoh Psamtik III, then besieged and took Memphis. Egypt became a Persian satrapy, and Libya and Cyrene submitted soon after.

events.name: Battle of Pelusium
events.text: Cambyses defeated Psamtik III's army and opened the road to the Nile.

events.name: Siege of Memphis
events.text: Memphis fell and Psamtik III was captured, ending the 26th Dynasty.

name: Greco-Persian Wars
summary: The Achaemenid Persian Empire fought Athens, Sparta and their allies after the Greek cities of Ionia rebelled against Persian rule with Athenian help. Two Persian invasions of mainland Greece were defeated, at Marathon in 490 BC and at Salamis and Plataea in 480 to 479 BC, and the Athenian-led Delian League then carried the war into Persian waters. The Greek victory preserved the independence of the city-states and opened the classical age of Athens.

steps.label: 499 to 494 BC
steps.title: Ionian Revolt
steps.text: Aristagoras of Miletus led the Greek cities of Ionia in revolt against their Persian-backed tyrants, and Athens and Eretria sent ships. The rebels marched inland and burned Sardis, the seat of the Persian satrap, in 498 BC. Persia slowly recovered the coast, destroyed the Ionian fleet off Lade and sacked Miletus, and Darius swore revenge on Athens.

moves.label: Ionians and Athenians march on Sardis

events.name: Burning of Sardis
events.text: The rebels burned the lower city of Sardis, which made Athens an enemy of Darius.

events.name: Battle of Lade
events.text: The Persian fleet crushed the Ionian navy after the Samians deserted, ending the revolt.

steps.label: 490 BC
steps.title: Marathon
steps.text: Darius sent a seaborne expedition under Datis and Artaphernes across the Aegean to punish Eretria and Athens. Eretria was betrayed and burned, but on the plain of Marathon the Athenians and Plataeans under Miltiades charged and routed the landing force. The Persian fleet sailed round to Athens, found the army back in the city and went home.

events.name: Sack of Eretria
events.text: Eretria fell after six days when traitors opened the gates.

events.name: Battle of Marathon
events.text: Miltiades' hoplites routed the Persian army on the shore and forced the expedition home.

steps.label: 480 BC
steps.title: Thermopylae and Artemisium
steps.text: Xerxes bridged the Hellespont and led a huge army and fleet along the coast of Thrace and Macedonia, which submitted. The allied Greeks held the narrow pass of Thermopylae on land and the Artemisium strait at sea. After three days a mountain path let the Persians outflank the pass; Leonidas and his Spartans died covering the retreat, and the Greek fleet fell back.

events.name: Battle of Thermopylae
events.text: Leonidas held the pass for three days before being surrounded and killed.

events.name: Battle of Artemisium
events.text: The Greek fleet fought the Persian navy to a standstill, then withdrew when the pass fell.

steps.label: September 480 BC
steps.title: Salamis
steps.text: The Persians marched through Boeotia and burned an evacuated Athens, while the Peloponnesians walled off the Isthmus of Corinth. Themistocles kept the allied fleet at Salamis and lured the Persian navy into the narrow straits, where it was shattered. Xerxes returned to Asia with much of his army, leaving Mardonius to finish the war.

events.name: Battle of Salamis
events.text: The Greek triremes destroyed the Persian fleet in the narrows, the turning point of the war.

steps.label: 479 BC
steps.title: Plataea and Mycale
steps.text: Mardonius wintered in Thessaly and came south again. The largest Greek army ever assembled, under the Spartan regent Pausanias, met him on the Asopus river and destroyed his army at Plataea, killing Mardonius. On the same day, by tradition, the Greek fleet landed at Mycale in Ionia and burned the Persian ships.

events.name: Battle of Plataea
events.text: Mardonius was killed and his army routed, ending the Persian invasion of Greece.

events.name: Battle of Mycale
events.text: The Greeks destroyed the beached Persian fleet, and Ionia rose again.

steps.label: 478 to 466 BC
steps.title: Delian League offensive
steps.text: Athens organised the Delian League to free the Greek cities of Asia and keep Persia out of the Aegean. Under Cimon the league fleet swept the coast of Asia Minor and won a double victory on land and sea at the Eurymedon river.

events.name: Battle of the Eurymedon
events.text: Cimon destroyed a Persian fleet and then its army at the river mouth in Pamphylia.

steps.label: 450 to 449 BC
steps.title: Cyprus and the Peace of Callias
steps.text: A last Athenian expedition fought for Cyprus, where Cimon died during the siege of Kition. After a victory off Salamis in Cyprus, fighting stopped, and later tradition holds that the Peace of Callias recognised the freedom of the Ionian Greeks.

events.name: Battle of Salamis in Cyprus
events.text: The Athenians beat a Phoenician and Cilician fleet and its army near Salamis in Cyprus.

events.name: Peace of Callias
events.text: A peace, attested only by later writers, ended open war between Athens and Persia.

name: Peloponnesian War
summary: Athens, a sea power ruling an Aegean empire, fought Sparta and its Peloponnesian League, a land power, for 27 years. Neither could strike the other's strength until Athens lost a great army in Sicily and Persia began paying for a Spartan fleet, which under Lysander destroyed the Athenian navy at Aegospotami. Athens surrendered in 404 BC, ending its empire, and the war left Greece exhausted and open to Persian, Theban and later Macedonian influence.

steps.label: 431 to 430 BC
steps.title: Pericles' strategy
steps.text: The war began when Thebes, Sparta's ally, attacked Athens' ally Plataea. King Archidamus II led the Peloponnesian army into Attica each summer to burn the farms, while Pericles brought the Athenians inside the Long Walls and sent the fleet to raid the Peloponnese. In 430 BC plague broke out in the crowded city and killed perhaps a quarter of the population, Pericles among them in 429 BC.

events.name: Invasion of Attica
events.text: The Spartans ravaged Attica while the Athenians watched from their walls.

events.name: Plague of Athens
events.text: An epidemic killed tens of thousands inside the overcrowded city.

steps.label: 425 BC
steps.title: Pylos and Sphacteria
steps.text: The Athenian general Demosthenes fortified the headland of Pylos on Sparta's own coast. Spartan troops landed on the island of Sphacteria to blockade him and were cut off by the Athenian fleet; Cleon and Demosthenes then stormed the island. The surrender of 292 men, about 120 of them full Spartan citizens, shocked Greece and gave Athens hostages that ended the invasions of Attica.

events.name: Battle of Sphacteria
events.text: Athenian light troops forced the surrender of the Spartan garrison on Sphacteria.

steps.label: 424 to 421 BC
steps.title: Delium, Amphipolis and the Peace of Nicias
steps.text: Athens' attempt to knock Boeotia out of the war failed at Delium. The Spartan Brasidas marched through Thessaly to Thrace and took Amphipolis, Athens' key colony, and in 422 BC both Brasidas and Cleon died in the battle to retake it. With the leading hawks gone, the Peace of Nicias in 421 BC restored the prewar position.

events.name: Battle of Delium
events.text: The Boeotians routed an Athenian army invading their territory.

events.name: Battle of Amphipolis
events.text: Brasidas defeated Cleon; both commanders were killed.

events.name: Peace of Nicias
events.text: A fifty-year peace that in practice lasted only a few years.

steps.label: 415 to 413 BC
steps.title: The Sicilian Expedition
steps.text: Persuaded by Alcibiades, Athens sent a huge fleet and army to conquer Syracuse, the greatest Greek city of Sicily. Alcibiades, recalled to face charges, fled to Sparta and advised it to send Gylippus to lead the defence. Reinforcements under Demosthenes could not break the siege, and in 413 BC the whole force was destroyed in the retreat; Nicias and Demosthenes were executed.

events.name: Siege of Syracuse
events.text: Gylippus broke the Athenian siege lines, and the Athenian fleet was beaten in the Great Harbour.

events.name: Disaster at the Assinarus
events.text: The retreating Athenian army was cut down at the river and the survivors sent to the quarries.

steps.label: 413 to 411 BC
steps.title: Decelea and Persian gold
steps.text: On Alcibiades' advice Sparta fortified Decelea in Attica, holding it year round and letting some 20,000 Athenian slaves escape from the silver mines. Athens' allies in Ionia revolted, and the Persian satrap Tissaphernes agreed to fund a Spartan fleet in return for the Greek cities of Asia. Athens rebuilt its navy from its last reserve fund.

events.name: Fortification of Decelea
events.text: A permanent Spartan fort in Attica cut Athens off from its land and mines.

events.name: Treaty of Miletus
events.text: Sparta traded the Greek cities of Asia for Persian money to build a fleet.

steps.label: 411 to 406 BC
steps.title: Athens strikes back at sea
steps.text: The war moved to the Hellespont, through which Athens' grain ships passed. Recalled by the fleet, Alcibiades won a crushing victory at Cyzicus in 410 BC, and in 406 BC the Athenians won again at Arginusae, though they executed six victorious generals for failing to rescue the drowning. Meanwhile Persia's prince Cyrus the Younger gave Lysander's fleet steady pay.

events.name: Battle of Cyzicus
events.text: Alcibiades destroyed the Peloponnesian fleet and killed its admiral Mindarus.

events.name: Battle of Arginusae
events.text: Athens won the largest naval battle of the war among Greeks.

steps.label: 405 to 404 BC
steps.title: Aegospotami and surrender
steps.text: Lysander took his Persian-funded fleet to the Hellespont and seized Lampsacus. The Athenian fleet beached opposite at Aegospotami, and Lysander caught most of it on the shore, capturing about 170 ships. Cut off from its grain, Athens was blockaded by land and sea and surrendered in April 404 BC; its Long Walls were torn down and the Thirty Tyrants installed.

events.name: Battle of Aegospotami
events.text: Lysander captured the Athenian fleet on the beach, deciding the war.

events.name: Surrender of Athens
events.text: Athens gave up its fleet and empire and accepted Spartan rule.

name: Rise of Macedon and the conquests of Alexander
summary: Philip II turned Macedon from a weak frontier kingdom into the dominant power in Greece, crowning his work by defeating Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BC. His son Alexander III led the Macedonian army and Greek allies against the Achaemenid Persian Empire, defeated Darius III at the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela, and marched on to Central Asia and the Indus. When Alexander died at Babylon in 323 BC his empire broke up among his generals, but Greek culture spread from Egypt to India in the Hellenistic age.

steps.label: 359 to 348 BC
steps.title: Philip builds Macedon
steps.text: Philip II took over a kingdom just beaten by the Illyrians and rebuilt its army around the long sarissa pike and the Companion cavalry. He crushed the Illyrian king Bardylis in 358 BC, seized Amphipolis and its gold mines, won Thessaly at the Crocus Field in 352 BC and destroyed Olynthus in 348 BC. In Athens, Demosthenes began warning that Philip meant to master all of Greece.

events.name: Defeat of Bardylis
events.text: Philip's new army killed thousands of Illyrians and secured Upper Macedonia.

events.name: Battle of the Crocus Field
events.text: Philip defeated the Phocians and became leader of Thessaly.

events.name: Fall of Olynthus
events.text: Philip razed Olynthus, Athens' ally in the north, and sold its people into slavery.

steps.label: 339 to 337 BC
steps.title: Chaeronea
steps.text: When Philip marched south into central Greece, Demosthenes persuaded Athens and Thebes to stand together. At Chaeronea in Boeotia, Philip drew the Athenians forward with a feigned retreat while the 18-year-old Alexander broke the Theban line and the Sacred Band. Philip then united the Greek cities except Sparta in the League of Corinth, with himself as leader of a planned war on Persia.

events.name: Battle of Chaeronea
events.text: Philip and Alexander destroyed the allied army of Athens and Thebes, ending Greek independence.

events.name: League of Corinth
events.text: The Greek cities swore alliance under Macedonian leadership for a war against Persia.

steps.label: 336 to 334 BC
steps.title: Alexander crosses into Asia
steps.text: Philip was murdered in 336 BC, and the young Alexander crushed a revolt by razing Thebes. In 334 BC he crossed the Hellespont with about 40,000 men and routed the western satraps at the Granicus river. He marched down the coast freeing the Greek cities and took Halicarnassus, defended by the mercenary general Memnon of Rhodes.

events.name: Destruction of Thebes
events.text: Alexander razed rebel Thebes as a warning to the rest of Greece.

events.name: Battle of the Granicus
events.text: Alexander led his cavalry across the river and routed the army of the western satraps.

events.name: Siege of Halicarnassus
events.text: Alexander took the city though Memnon's garrison held out in its citadels.

steps.label: 333 BC
steps.title: Issus
steps.text: After cutting the Gordian knot, Alexander passed through the Cilician Gates to the Syrian coast. Darius III brought the royal army from Babylon and came down behind him, but on the narrow plain of Issus Alexander's cavalry charge broke the Persian line. Darius fled, leaving his mother, wife and children in Macedonian hands.

events.name: Battle of Issus
events.text: Alexander's charge broke the Persian line and Darius fled the field.

steps.label: 332 to 331 BC
steps.title: Tyre and Egypt
steps.text: Rather than chase Darius, Alexander took the Mediterranean ports to neutralise the Persian fleet. Tyre fell after a seven-month siege and a mole built out to the island city, Gaza followed, and Egypt welcomed him as pharaoh. He founded Alexandria and visited the oracle of Ammon at Siwa.

events.name: Siege of Tyre
events.text: Alexander built a causeway to the island fortress and stormed it after seven months.

events.name: Siege of Gaza
events.text: Gaza fell after two months, opening the road to Egypt.

events.name: Founding of Alexandria
events.text: The new city became the greatest port and centre of learning of the Hellenistic world.

steps.label: 331 to 330 BC
steps.title: Gaugamela and the fall of Persia
steps.text: Alexander crossed the Euphrates and Tigris to meet Darius' last great army on open ground near Gaugamela, and his oblique attack split the Persian line. Babylon and Susa surrendered, Alexander forced the Persian Gates and burned the palaces of Persepolis. Darius fled east and was murdered by his own satrap Bessus before Alexander could catch him.

events.name: Battle of Gaugamela
events.text: The decisive defeat of Darius III, which effectively ended Achaemenid rule.

events.name: Burning of Persepolis
events.text: Alexander's army burned the ceremonial palaces of the Persian kings.

events.name: Death of Darius III
events.text: Bessus killed the fleeing king, and Alexander claimed his throne.

steps.label: 329 to 326 BC
steps.title: Bactria, Sogdiana and India
steps.text: Alexander crossed the Hindu Kush, caught Bessus and fought a hard guerrilla war against Spitamenes in Sogdiana, ending it by marrying the Sogdian noblewoman Roxana. He then entered the Punjab, where Taxila submitted, and beat King Porus and his war elephants at the Hydaspes. At the Hyphasis river his exhausted army refused to go further.

moves.label: Over the Hindu Kush into Sogdiana

events.name: Battle of the Jaxartes
events.text: Alexander crossed the river under catapult cover and routed the Scythian horse archers.

events.name: Battle of the Hydaspes
events.text: Alexander crossed the swollen river by night and defeated Porus, whom he kept as a vassal king.

events.name: Mutiny at the Hyphasis
events.text: The army refused to march further east, and Alexander turned back.

steps.label: 325 to 323 BC
steps.title: Return and death
steps.text: The army sailed and marched down the Indus, then Alexander led part of it through the Gedrosian desert with heavy losses while Nearchus took the fleet along the coast to the Persian Gulf. Back in Babylon, Alexander planned new campaigns but died there in June 323 BC, aged 32, with no adult heir. His generals divided the empire and fought over it for forty years.

events.name: Gedrosian desert march
events.text: Thirst and heat killed a large part of the army and its followers.

events.name: Death of Alexander
events.text: Alexander died of fever at Babylon, and his empire passed to his quarrelling generals.

name: Warring States and the Qin unification of China
summary: After the Zhou kings lost real power, seven large territorial states, Qin, Chu, Qi, Zhao, Wei, Han and Yan, fought for two and a half centuries with mass infantry armies and ever larger battles. Qin, on the western frontier, reformed itself under Shang Yang into a disciplined war state, broke its rivals one by one under generals such as Bai Qi, and between 230 and 221 BC King Ying Zheng conquered all six. He proclaimed himself Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor, founding the unified imperial China that lasted two thousand years.

steps.label: 475 to 403 BC
steps.title: The partition of Jin
steps.text: The old great state of Jin was dominated by rival ministerial clans. In 453 BC the Zhi clan, besieging the Zhao at Jinyang, was betrayed by its allies Han and Wei, who joined Zhao to destroy it. Zhao, Han and Wei divided Jin among themselves and were recognised as states in 403 BC, the usual start of the Warring States era. The map's border data shows all the Chinese states as one polity before the 320s BC.

events.name: Siege of Jinyang
events.text: Han and Wei turned on the Zhi clan, and the three survivors partitioned Jin.

steps.label: 356 to 340 BC
steps.title: Shang Yang's reforms and the fall of Wei
steps.text: Wei was the strongest state in the early 4th century BC. In Qin, Duke Xiao's minister Shang Yang abolished hereditary privilege, rewarded soldiers by heads taken and organised the peasants into a war economy. Wei's general Pang Juan was then destroyed by the Qi strategist Sun Bin at Maling in 341 BC, and the next year Shang Yang's Qin army took Wei's lands west of the Yellow River.

moves.label: Wei army turns back from Han
Qin attack on Wei's Hexi lands

events.name: Battle of Maling
events.text: Sun Bin ambushed and destroyed the Wei army, and Pang Juan was killed; the exact site is disputed.

events.name: Qin takes Hexi
events.text: Shang Yang beat Wei, which soon moved its capital east to Daliang.

steps.label: 318 to 316 BC
steps.title: Hangu Pass and the conquest of Shu
steps.text: Diplomats preached rival strategies: a vertical alliance of the eastern states against Qin, or horizontal alliances with Qin. In 318 BC a coalition led by Wei, Zhao, Han, Yan and Chu attacked the Hangu Pass and was thrown back. In 316 BC the Qin general Sima Cuo crossed the Qinling mountains and conquered Shu and Ba in Sichuan, giving Qin a vast and safe granary.

events.name: Coalition defeated at Hangu Pass
events.text: Qin held its eastern gateway and routed the allied armies.

events.name: Qin conquest of Shu
events.text: The rich Sichuan basin became Qin's base for wars against Chu.

steps.label: 293 BC
steps.title: Bai Qi at Yique
steps.text: Qin's greatest general, Bai Qi, first made his name against Han and Wei. At Yique, the gorge south of Luoyang, he defeated their combined army and, by Qin's own count, killed 240,000 men. From now on Qin bit off the Yellow River lands of its eastern neighbours piece by piece.

moves.label: Allied army of Han and Wei

events.name: Battle of Yique
events.text: Bai Qi annihilated the allied army of Han and Wei.

steps.label: 284 to 279 BC
steps.title: Yue Yi breaks Qi
steps.text: Qi had grown rich and aggressive under King Min. In 284 BC an alliance of Yan, Qin, Zhao, Wei and Han, led by the Yan general Yue Yi, routed Qi and sacked its capital Linzi, leaving only two Qi cities unconquered. Qi's commander Tian Dan broke out of Jimo in 279 BC with a famous attack by oxen with burning tails and recovered the state, but Qi never again threatened Qin.

events.name: Sack of Linzi
events.text: Yue Yi's coalition took the Qi capital, removing the one eastern power that rivalled Qin.

events.name: Fire oxen of Jimo
events.text: Tian Dan routed the Yan besiegers and Qi recovered its lost cities.

steps.label: 279 to 278 BC
steps.title: Bai Qi sacks Ying
steps.text: Qin now turned on Chu, the largest state, attacking down the Han river from the north and from Sichuan in the west. Bai Qi flooded the city of Yan by diverting a river and in 278 BC took the Chu capital Ying, burning the royal tombs. The Chu court fled east to Chen, and Qin held the middle Yangtze.

events.name: Sack of Ying
events.text: Qin captured the Chu capital and turned its lands into Nan commandery.

steps.label: 262 to 256 BC
steps.title: Changping and the end of Zhou
steps.text: Qin and Zhao fought for the Shangdang upland. At Changping, Zhao replaced the cautious Lian Po with the young Zhao Kuo, who attacked, was surrounded by Bai Qi and starved for 46 days; Qin then killed most of the 400,000 prisoners, by tradition. Qin's siege of the Zhao capital Handan was broken in 257 BC by relief armies from Wei and Chu, but in 256 BC Qin ended the last Zhou king's line.

events.name: Battle of Changping
events.text: Bai Qi destroyed the main Zhao army, the bloodiest battle of the era.

events.name: Relief of Handan
events.text: Wei and Chu armies forced Qin to lift its siege of the Zhao capital.

events.name: End of the Zhou dynasty
events.text: Qin absorbed the tiny royal domain, ending the Zhou line after eight centuries.

steps.label: 230 to 225 BC
steps.title: Han, Zhao and Wei fall
steps.text: King Ying Zheng of Qin launched the final wars. Neishi Teng took the Han capital in 230 BC. Wang Jian invaded Zhao, which executed its best general Li Mu after Qin bribery, and Handan fell in 228 BC. In 225 BC Wang Ben flooded the Wei capital Daliang with the Yellow River until its walls collapsed.

events.name: Fall of Handan
events.text: Qin captured the Zhao capital and King Qian of Zhao.

events.name: Siege of Daliang
events.text: Qin flooded the Wei capital, modern Kaifeng, and forced its surrender.

steps.label: 225 to 221 BC
steps.title: Chu, Yan and Qi: unification
steps.text: Chu destroyed a first Qin invasion under Li Xin, so the king gave the veteran Wang Jian 600,000 men; he waited out Chu in fortified camps, then struck and killed its general Xiang Yan, taking Shouchun in 223 BC. Wang Ben finished off Yan in Liaodong and the Zhao remnant of Dai in 222 BC, and in 221 BC Qi surrendered without a battle. Ying Zheng took the new title Shi Huangdi, the First Emperor.

events.name: Battle of Qinan
events.text: Wang Jian destroyed the main Chu army; Xiang Yan was killed.

events.name: Fall of Shouchun
events.text: Qin captured the Chu capital and King Fuchu, ending Chu as a state.

events.name: Surrender of Qi
events.text: King Jian of Qi gave up without a fight, completing the unification of China.

name: Kalinga War
summary: The Mauryan emperor Ashoka invaded Kalinga, an independent kingdom on the Bay of Bengal coast in modern Odisha, around the eighth year of his reign. The conquest succeeded, but by Ashoka's own inscription some 100,000 people were killed and 150,000 deported. Ashoka's remorse turned him toward Buddhism and a policy of rule by dharma that he proclaimed on rock and pillar edicts across India.

sides.name: Kalinga
leaders: Kalinga army (rulers unnamed in the sources)

steps.label: c. 262 BC
steps.title: Ashoka turns on Kalinga
steps.text: Ashoka had inherited from his father Bindusara and grandfather Chandragupta an empire covering almost all of the subcontinent. Kalinga, a rich coastal kingdom between the Mahanadi and Godavari rivers with its own large army and sea trade, stayed outside it and controlled the routes to the south. The map's border data already includes Kalinga in the Mauryan Empire, so the frontier line marks the independent kingdom.

steps.label: c. 261 BC
steps.title: Conquest of Kalinga
steps.text: The Mauryan army broke into Kalinga and took its heartland around Tosali, near modern Bhubaneswar. Local tradition places the decisive battle near the Dhauli hills on the Daya river, though no ancient source names the site. Ashoka's thirteenth rock edict counts 150,000 people deported, 100,000 killed and many times that number dead of other causes.

moves.label: Kalinga forces fall back on Tosali

events.name: Battle of Kalinga (Dhauli, by tradition)
events.text: Ashoka's army crushed Kalinga's resistance at enormous human cost.

steps.label: c. 260 BC onward
steps.title: Ashoka's remorse
steps.text: Kalinga became a Mauryan province governed from Tosali. In his edicts Ashoka wrote that he felt deep sorrow for the suffering of the conquest, renounced further war, and turned to Buddhism and dharma, a code of nonviolence, tolerance and welfare. Edicts carved at Dhauli and Jaugada told Kalinga's officials to treat the people justly, and Ashoka sent Buddhist missions across Asia.

events.name: Kalinga edicts
events.text: Special rock edicts at Dhauli and Jaugada set out Ashoka's new policy for the conquered land.
